summary:
Both shelves are sorted, so the smallest remaining book is always at the front of one of them. Compare the two
fronts, take the smaller, advance that pointer; when one shelf runs out, append the rest of the other.
O(n + m).

question.md:
Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list.

- **Either list can be empty** (but not both).
- **Equal heights** can appear in both.
- **Up to 10⁵ each.**

think.md:
`[2, 5, 9, 12]` and `[1, 5, 7, 15, 20]` merge into `[1, 2, 5, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20]`.

The first merged book must be the smaller of the two front books. After taking it, the same is true of what's
left. So a single pass with one pointer per list builds the merge.

idea.md: Join the two lists and sort.

lines.text: Everything together, then a general sort.

complexity.md: **Time O((n + m) log(n + m)).** **Space O(n + m).**

walk.title: Put both shelves together and sort.

limits.md: Throws away the fact that each shelf is already sorted. Merging uses it to finish in one linear pass.

idea.md: `i` on `left`, `j` on `right`. While both have books, append the smaller front (`left` on ties). Then append the remainder.

lines.text: Output and one pointer per shelf.
The smaller front is the next smallest book overall; `<=` takes from the left first on ties.
One shelf ran out; the other's remaining books are all larger and already in order.

complexity.md: **Time O(n + m).** **Space O(n + m)** for the output.

steps.text: One shelf is empty; append the rest: [1, 2, 5, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20].

walk.title: One pointer per shelf. Take the shorter front book each time (the left one on ties); when a shelf runs out, take the rest of the other.

takeaways.md:
- **Merging two sorted lists:** compare fronts, take the smaller, linear time.
- It's the step merge sort is built on, and it extends to k lists with a heap.
- Don't forget the leftovers after the loop.
